That's not quite the right way to think about it. You're thinking of the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics, because that is what implies the whole "each of my decisions goes every possible way" bit, and your universe clones do each possible thing.

This isn't like that. You're only as likely to eat cat shit as the "real universe" is to care what happens if you eat cat shit under various circumstances.

The simulations are under no obligation to be different. It could be that this exact simulated universe was run a hundred billion times, or perhaps only a narrow band of possibilities are explored.

But to say, "as a random human being, I'm probably not part of the un-simulated world" is the same as saying "as a random human being, I'm probably not going to witness the assassination of Lincoln". In all the time periods in which humans exist, you could be any one of those people, and those that did not see lincoln's death far, far outnumber those that did.

1) If you accept that technology will eventually be able to simulate an entire universe like our own, go to 2.

2) If you accept that these simulations are likely to number in the hundreds of thousands or more, go to 3.

3) If every real universe has hundreds of thousands of simulated universes, what are the odds that you exist in a non-simulated universe?

The odds are actually much worse than hundreds of thousands to one. Simulations on all kinds of things are done hundreds of thousands of times per day across the globe. Every single iteration of a universe from beginning to end could be played out in seconds - looped over and over again for months in order to get data for some thing or another... or maybe for people to play with.

Combine this with 4) technology might eventually be able to extend lifespans indefinitely and you'd have a lot of bored people eager to rediscover the urgency of a mortal 'life' within a simulation. So when you die, the first thing you see is a scoreboard?

There's another reason a civilization might run simulations, though. It's possible that we become hidebound, paralyzed even, by preconceptions as society becomes more complex. Maybe simulations in which new societies are unfolding (while being observed from outside of the simulation), not trapped by existing ideas, could lead to new ideas, discoveries, forms of art, and so on.
